## VAL-1203 comes back executed

Last module, VAL-1203's draft validation plan went back for revision: an untestable URS (user
requirements specification — what the system has to do, in plain business language) row, a
blank risk ranking on the release-gate requirement, and no row at all for the in-house
LIS-to-BECS (laboratory information system to Blood Establishment Computer Software) translation
script. Weeks later, the executed package is back on your desk: IQ, OQ, and PQ evidence
(installation, operational, and performance qualification — industry's own names for three test
stages, defined properly below), a traceability matrix, and a validation summary report.

Your Quality Analyst (QA) reviewed it first, same as always. She caught one gap herself before
it reached you — worth saying plainly, because it's true: she's gotten sharper at this since the
work you did together last course, and this package proves it. But she also flagged, honestly,
that she couldn't fully judge whether the testing was *enough* — that's still the Quality
Validation Lead's call to own, and increasingly yours to review.

Here's the excerpt that reached both of you. It was written by the Validation Lead and the
vendor's implementation consultant. Before you read anything else in this lesson, read it the
way you'd read any package cold, and try to find what's wrong with it yourself.

> **VAL-1203 — Executed Validation Package (excerpt)**
>
> *Traceability matrix (partial)*
>
> | Req ID | Requirement (risk) | Test ID(s) | Result |
> |---|---|---|---|
> | REQ-022 | System shall not permit release of a blood component until all required test results for that donation are recorded as complete. (Risk: High) | OQ-114 | Pass |
> | REQ-031 | System shall classify an infectious-disease marker result as nonreactive, reactive, or invalid based on the assay's signal-to-cutoff (S/CO) ratio. (Risk: High) | OQ-128 | Pass |
> | REQ-045 | LIS-to-BECS translation script shall correctly map each incoming result field to BECS's expected input format. (Risk: High) | — | — |
>
> *Selected OQ/PQ results*
>
> **OQ-114** — Input: donation with all three required infectious-disease markers resulted and
> recorded. Expected: component release permitted. Actual: release permitted. Pass.
>
> **OQ-128** — Input: S/CO 0.40 (clearly nonreactive). Expected: system classifies
> "Nonreactive." Actual: "Nonreactive." Pass.
>
> **OQ-142** — Quarantine hold enforcement. Input: donation with one marker still pending.
> Expected: release blocked. Actual (first run): release permitted — **FAIL**. Logged as
> Validation Deviation VD-003; root cause: a configuration timeout released the hold before the
> pending-result flag posted. Fixed; re-tested two days later. Actual (re-run): release blocked.
> Pass. VD-003 referenced in Section 6 of this report.
>
> **PQ-07** — Peak concurrent load / intended-use performance. Performed in the vendor's staging
> environment, by the vendor's implementation staff, using the vendor's standard test dataset,
> business hours only. Expected and actual system response times within spec. Pass.
>
> **IQ-02** — Installed application server: Release B, build 4.2.118. Database engine version
> 14.3.
>
> *Validation Summary Report, Section 7 — Conclusion*: "Testing demonstrates BECS Release B
> meets its requirements. One deviation (VD-007, Fairview label-print timing, root cause under
> investigation) remains open. The system is validated and ready for routine production use."
> Approvals: Quality Validation Lead (signed, dated). Director, IT Service Operations
> (signature line present, no date).

One more thing is sitting on your second monitor, not in the package at all: the BECS change
record from cutover weekend, pulled from the CMDB (configuration management database — the
system of record for what's actually deployed). It lists the database engine promoted to
production as version **14.4.2**. IQ-02 above tested version 14.3.

Go find what's wrong before you read on. You should be able to name at least four or five
distinct problems, one thing that looks wrong but isn't, and one thing nobody without your
background would catch at all.

## Why this matters, and the ITSM bridge

The failure this package is supposed to prevent isn't "the testing didn't happen." It's
quieter: testing happened, it looks thorough, everyone signed it, and it still didn't prove the
system does what it needs to do under the conditions it will actually face. A package that looks
finished and a package that proves something are not the same document, and the gap between them
is where a defect reaches a patient without anyone noticing until an inspector — or a
transfusion reaction — finds it first.

You already run this discipline under different names. **Test management and release
acceptance** is the ITSM (IT service management) practice of defining test plans, entry and exit
criteria, triaging defects, and tracking requirements traceability inside an ALM (application
lifecycle management — the tooling that tracks requirements, builds, and test cases together)
tool. This course's own loose mapping, not an official one anywhere: IQ sits roughly where
**build and deployment verification against a configuration baseline** sits — did the thing
that's supposed to be running actually get installed as specified. OQ sits roughly where
**functional and system testing** sits — does each function work. PQ sits roughly where
**operational acceptance and performance testing under real conditions** sits — does it hold up
under load, with real users.

Where the regulated world demands more: in ordinary release management, exit criteria sometimes
flex once you see how testing went — a team under schedule pressure adjusts "done" to match
what got finished. In validation, criteria are fixed *before* execution and never adjusted
afterward to fit the results. Every failure gets dispositioned in writing, not quietly re-run and
forgotten. And the evidence has to be something an outsider — an inspector, a new hire, you in a
year — can read cold and still follow, without the author in the room.

## The rule in plain English

**IQ, OQ, and PQ are industry vocabulary, not FDA regulation or FDA guidance language.** FDA's
BECS guidance (*Blood Establishment Computer System Validation in the User's Facility*, CBER,
April 2013 — the same guidance module 1 used, tier: **guidance**, not binding) never uses the
terms "IQ," "OQ," or "PQ." Industry built this three-way packaging as a clean way to organize
what the guidance actually recommends. Here's this course's own labeled mapping onto the
guidance's own sections — label it that way whenever you use it, because nobody outside industry
practice is required to organize a package this way:

- **IQ (installation qualification)** — does the installed, configured system match what was
  specified? This lines up with what the guidance's system-documentation section (III.B)
  recommends you maintain: operating system and version number, the list of interfaces, the list
  of environments (test, training, production), hardware specifications, and more.
- **OQ (operational qualification)** — does each function actually work, under the full range of
  conditions a function should be tested against? This lines up with the guidance's validation
  activities section (III.G): normal, abnormal, boundary, and "absurd" inputs, plus security-role
  testing.
- **PQ (performance qualification)** — does the system meet its intended use, running at
  Lakeshore's own location, under Lakeshore's own conditions? This lines up with the guidance's
  scope-of-validation section (III.D): your own SOPs (standard operating procedures), your own
  personnel, your own hardware, at peak concurrent load, with your report outputs verified.

Two of the guidance's own definitions are worth having exactly, because they're the closest
thing it offers to OQ and PQ in its own words (tier: **guidance**, quoted from
`sources/fda-guidance/becs-validation-users-facility-2013.md`):

> Qualification operational means establishing confidence that process equipment and sub-systems
> are capable of consistently operating within established limits and tolerances (Ref. 3).

> User validation means testing new equipment or a new process in the environment where it will
> be used to ensure that it will reliably produce a product that meets pre-determined
> qualifications and quality standards (Ref. 4).

Read those against the mapping above: "operating within established limits and tolerances" is
OQ's job. "In the environment where it will be used" is PQ's job, almost word for word.

### A second layer of review: the adequacy check

`directing-the-quality-analyst` gave you the **cold-read test** (name only, not re-taught here):
would this document survive an inspector reading it cold, a year from now, with its author not
in the room — checked against conclusion, evidence, reasoning, criteria set first, decision
trail, and loose ends. That test tells you whether the package's *story* holds together. It
doesn't tell you whether the *testing itself* was any good.

This course adds a second instrument for that: the **adequacy check**. Four questions, each
drawn from FDA's BECS guidance (tier: guidance, cited by section below). You'll use all four
across this course; this module applies the first three to VAL-1203's excerpt. The fourth,
Regression, is module 6's full subject — named here so you know it exists, not applied yet.

1. **Coverage.** Does every requirement touching a critical function trace to at least one test,
   with the highest-risk functions tested most thoroughly? (Guidance III.E.)
2. **Design.** Could each test actually fail? Expected results fixed in advance, plus normal,
   abnormal, boundary, and "absurd" inputs, and worst-case load. (Guidance III.D and III.G.)
3. **Fidelity.** Was it tested where and how it will really run — Lakeshore's own location,
   configuration, software, hardware, SOPs, and personnel, at peak load? (Guidance III.D and
   III.G.)
4. **Regression.** For a change: is there a documented analysis of the change's impact on the
   *whole* system, with regression testing that follows from that analysis? (Guidance III.I —
   name only here. Module 6 is where you apply it.)

## Citation decoder

| Citation | How to read it aloud | What it requires | In our scenario |
|---|---|---|---|
| Guidance III.B | "Section three, part B" | Recommends a documentation list: OS and version, interfaces, environments, hardware specs, and more. | Maps to what VAL-1203's IQ record should have captured — and where the version mismatch hides. |
| Guidance III.D | "Section three, part D" | Recommends validating at your own location with your own software, hardware, SOPs, and personnel, including worst-case load. | The Fidelity question — and PQ-07's exact failure. |
| Guidance III.E | "Section three, part E" | Recommends testing the highest-risk functions most comprehensively. | The Coverage question — and REQ-022's single normal-case test. |
| Guidance III.F | "Section three, part F" | Recommends validation SOPs, including one for "Handling validation deviations." | The standard VD-003 and VD-007 are judged against. |
| Guidance III.G | "Section three, part G" | Recommends test-case anatomy, normal/abnormal/boundary/absurd inputs, record retention, screen-print linkage, promoting the validated configuration to production. | The Design question — and OQ-128's missing boundary case. |
| Guidance III.H | "Section three, part H" | Requires documenting validation activities (21 CFR 211.68, 211.100(b), 606.160(b)(5)); recommends the report include variances, amendments, and dated management approvals. | VAL-1203's conclusion and its undated approval line. |
| 21 CFR 211.68(a), cited by the guidance | "Two-eleven point sixty-eight, paragraph a" | A written program must require validation prior to routine use — not deployment first, sign-off after. | Why VAL-1203 can't go to production with Section 7's open deviation. |

## The actual text

On what the IQ record should cover, FDA's guidance (tier: **guidance**) recommends, among other
things, that you document:

> Operating system and version number... List of interfaces; and List of environments on system,
> e.g., test, training, production, etc.

That's the IQ side of VAL-1203's gap: a version record exists, it's just not the version that
ended up in production.

On risk-scaling test depth — the Coverage question's own words:

> The highest risk functions of the system should be tested more comprehensively. For example,
> because of the potentially fatal consequences of a transfusion based on an improper crossmatch
> between donor and recipient, the validation of the electronic or computer crossmatch would
> require more extensive testing.

On what makes a test able to fail — the Design question's own words, including its own
boundary-testing example:

> Boundary testing is testing at the boundary of a specification, in other words, at the limit,
> just below the limit, and just over the limit. Boundary values are "off-by-one errors." An
> example of boundary testing is testing for a hematocrit of 37%, 38% and 39% if the cutoff (or
> boundary value) for hematocrit is 38%.

And on absurd values:

> Examples of absurd or unexpected values might be an alpha result in a numeric field, a
> hematocrit of 110% or a blank (or leading blank) in a result field.

Every executed test case, per the guidance, carries a fixed anatomy, with screen prints linked
back to the case that produced them:

> Each executed test case in your pre-defined written test plan should include the input,
> expected output, actual output, acceptance criteria, whether the test passed or failed, the
> name or initials of the person performing the test, and the date the test was performed.

> For traceability purposes and to facilitate quality assurance review and follow-up, we
> recommend that any supporting documentation, such as screen-prints, where appropriate, be
> identified to link them to the specific test case.

On where PQ has to happen, and at what load — the Fidelity question's own words:

> You should validate your system at your location using the same software, hardware, SOPs, and
> personnel who will use the system after it is formally implemented.

> The test cases should include those that represent "worst case scenarios," e.g., maximum
> numbers of users working simultaneously, all possible activities occurring simultaneously, etc.

"Handling validation deviations" is named directly in the guidance's own list of recommended
validation-SOP topics (III.F), alongside "Writing test cases," "Amending test cases," and
"Validating after a change." And on the report itself:

> Your validation report should include a summary of the test results, including any variances
> or failed tests, any amendments made to the test cases or the validation plan, an evaluation of
> the outcome of your testing, and approvals or sign-offs by management, including dates.

On when a validated system is actually allowed to go live — this sentence is citing regulation
(21 CFR 211.68(a)) inside a guidance document, the "must" the guidance flags everywhere versus
its own "should":

> A written plan is not "designed to assure proper performance" unless it requires user
> validation prior to routine use, on a routine basis, and any time a change is made that has the
> potential to affect the functions of the system.

On retention — named here as what the guidance says you must keep, not re-quoted from the
underlying CFR text itself (that got its own treatment earlier in this curriculum):

> You must retain validation records (21 CFR 211.68(b), 211.100(b), 606.160(b)(5)(ii)). Your
> records should include documented evidence of all test cases, test input data and test
> results. Test results should include screen prints.

And on moving a validated configuration into production — the sentence behind the Director-only
catch:

> We recommend that you perform validation in the "test environment" or "test partition" of your
> system. After successful validation, you or your software manufacturer should copy or move the
> file configuration on which you performed your validation into the production environment.

AABB's Quality System Essentials (QSE) framework, paraphrased only, no standard number: this
kind of qualification work sits under **QSE 3, Equipment** — explicitly including IT systems, not
just physical lab equipment — alongside **QSE 5, Process Control**, the same theme module 1
named for validation generally.

## Reading VAL-1203 cold

Here's what the excerpt actually shows, organized the way you should organize any review: the
cold-read test first, then the adequacy check's three applied questions.

**Decision trail (cold-read).** The conclusion says "validated and ready for routine production
use" while VD-007 sits open, root cause "under investigation," with no disposition. A conclusion
that outruns its own evidence is exactly what the cold-read test catches. The Director's approval
line also has no date — the guidance's report section asks for "approvals or sign-offs by
management, including dates" (III.H) so a signature can prove *when* it happened: before or
after that open deviation, before or after deployment. Both are gaps to flag before signing.

**Coverage.** REQ-022, the release-gate requirement — correctly risk-ranked this time, unlike
module 1's draft — traces to exactly one test, OQ-114, a normal-case test: every result present
and complete, release permitted. Nothing tests the boundary (one result still pending) or a
failure condition. A high-risk requirement with only a happy-path test behind it hasn't been
proven to do its one job: refuse release when it should.

**Design.** REQ-031 governs a field with a real clinical cutoff — an S/CO (signal-to-cutoff)
ratio, the kind of result an infectious-disease marker assay reports, where a ratio at or above
the assay's threshold reads "reactive" and below it reads "nonreactive." OQ-128 tested exactly
one value, 0.40, comfortably nonreactive. Nothing tests at the boundary, nothing tests an absurd
value (non-numeric, out-of-range), and nothing tests an "invalid" result. A test that can only
ever pass, because it was never aimed near where the logic could break, isn't proof. It's a
formality wearing a test case's row number.

**Fidelity.** PQ-07, the peak-load and intended-use test, ran in the vendor's own staging
environment, with the vendor's own staff, using the vendor's own dataset, during business hours.
III.D's whole point is to validate "at your location using the same software, hardware, SOPs, and
personnel who will use the system after it is formally implemented" — and at worst-case load, not
a quiet weekday. This test proves the vendor's environment behaves. It doesn't prove
Lakeshore's does.

**Traceability (orphan).** REQ-045 — the in-house LIS-to-BECS translation script, finally given
its own URS row after module 1 flagged its absence entirely — has no test ID at all. The row
exists now; nothing traces to it. The one component with the least outside scrutiny behind it is
still the one component nobody has actually tested.

**Director-only catch.** IQ-02 records the database engine tested as version 14.3. The BECS
change record from cutover weekend — in the CMDB, not the validation package — shows version
14.4.2 as what was actually promoted to production. The guidance's own instruction is to validate
in test and then "copy or move the file configuration on which you performed your validation into
the production environment" (III.G). What ran in test and what's running now have to be provably
the same thing; here they aren't. Nobody outside IT would think to pull the change record and
cross-check it against the IQ sheet — but you would, because the CMDB is where "what's actually
running" lives, and the package is only where "what we claim we tested" lives.

**The non-gap.** OQ-142 failed on its first run. That's not, by itself, a problem — if you
flagged it as one, reread it. It was logged as Validation Deviation VD-003, root-caused (a
configuration timeout releasing the hold before the pending-result flag posted), fixed, and
re-tested, with VD-003 referenced in the report. That's the guidance's deviation-SOP expectation
(III.F) working as intended — the mirror image of VIA-0842's step 7 earlier in this curriculum, a
test that failed and was silently re-run to green with no discrepancy note. Here the same kind of
failure got the documentation treatment VIA-0842's didn't. Done this way, it's not a
decision-trail concern. It's the system working.

Five gaps, one non-gap, one catch only your background would make — a package that looks
finished in several places and proves something in only some of them.

## What an inspector would actually look for

An FDA investigator or AABB assessor reading VAL-1203's file wouldn't stop at "there's a
traceability matrix, there's test evidence, there are signatures." They'd pull three threads:
does every high-risk requirement's test actually exercise the failure mode the requirement exists
to prevent (not "is there a test," but "could this specific test have failed if the software were
broken" — REQ-022's single normal-case trace fails that even though the row, the test, and the
"Pass" all exist); does the IQ record match what's actually deployed in production right now
(the cheapest check in the file, and the one most reviewers skip, because it means pulling a
second document — a version mismatch here means the whole package hasn't been shown to describe
the system actually running); and is every deviation dispositioned before the report declares
success ("validated and ready for production use" next to an open, un-root-caused deviation is
the kind of sentence an inspector reads once and writes down).

A bad answer to "why does the report say validated with an open deviation" sounds like "that one
was minor, we were confident it'd resolve fine." A good answer is: there is no good answer. It
gets fixed before the report is final, not explained away after.

## Common traps

**"IQ, OQ, and PQ are each their own separate regulatory requirement, so the package is
noncompliant without three distinct documents."** No FDA regulation or guidance sentence uses
those three terms — the text quoted above talks about a validation plan, test-case anatomy,
records, and a report. IQ/OQ/PQ packaging is industry's own way of organizing that content into
a teachable structure. A package that proves installation matches spec, every function was
tested under real conditions, and the system performs as intended at Lakeshore has satisfied the
substance, whatever headings it uses. What genuinely *is* required: retaining the records
themselves, and the guidance says so by citing actual regulation — 211.68(b), 211.100(b), and
606.160(b)(5)(ii) — not by recommending it.

**"The test passed, so the requirement is proven."** A pass only means something if the test
could have failed. OQ-128's single nonreactive value and OQ-114's single complete-donation case
both "passed," and both prove almost nothing — neither input was ever going to produce a fail
result. A pass against a test never aimed at the failure mode isn't evidence. It's a box checked
next to a row number.

## What this means for your job

- **Read the traceability matrix in both directions.** Forward: does every requirement touching
  a critical function have at least one test? Backward: does every test actually tie back to a
  real requirement, or is some of it effort spent proving nothing anyone asked for? An orphan in
  either direction is a gap, not a formatting issue.
- **For every "Pass," ask what result would have produced a "Fail."** If you can't answer that in
  one sentence, the test wasn't designed to fail, and the pass tells you nothing.
- **Cross-check the IQ record against the CMDB and the change record, every time.** This is the
  one check a non-technical reviewer will reliably skip, and it's cheap: does the version tested
  match the version actually promoted to production? If they don't match, nothing else in the
  package can be trusted until that's reconciled.
- **Never let a report's conclusion outrun its open items.** "Validated" and an undispositioned
  deviation can't coexist in the same sentence. Send it back before co-signing, not after.
- **When a test failed and was fixed, check that it's documented that way — not treat every
  failure as automatically suspicious.** A logged deviation, a root cause, a fix, and a re-test
  that references the deviation is the system working as designed. Learn to recognize that
  pattern so you spend your scrutiny on the gaps that actually matter.

## Check your understanding

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q1: Someone on the upgrade project says, "FDA requires separate IQ, OQ, and PQ documents, so if VAL-1203 doesn't have three distinct, separately labeled packages, it's out of compliance." Accurate?

No. Go back to the guidance text quoted in this lesson: it asks for a validation plan, defined
test-case contents, retained records, and a report — it never names "IQ," "OQ," or "PQ." That
three-way packaging is industry practice, used here because it's a clear, teachable structure,
not because any regulation or FDA guidance mandates it by name. What *is* actually required,
named exactly as such: retaining the validation records themselves. The guidance cites regulation
for that — 21 CFR 211.68(b), 211.100(b), and 606.160(b)(5)(ii) — not a recommendation. So the
headings are optional. Keeping the records isn't.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q2: Of the gaps in VAL-1203's excerpt, one item — OQ-142 — isn't actually a defect. What makes it different from the others?

OQ-142 failed on its first run, same as a real defect would. The difference is everything that
happened next: logged as a validation deviation (VD-003), root-caused to a configuration
timeout, fixed, re-tested, with the deviation referenced in the final report — the guidance's
own expectation for handling validation deviations (III.F), done correctly. Compare it to
VIA-0842's step 7 earlier in this curriculum, where a failed test was silently re-run to green
with no discrepancy note — same surface event, opposite handling. Flagging OQ-142 would mean
punishing the behavior you want more of. The real gaps are the ones that look clean on the
surface, like REQ-022's single passing test, not the one honest about having failed once.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q3: IQ-02 says the database engine tested was version 14.3. Nothing in the matrix or the report flags that line. Why is it a gap anyway?

A second record — the BECS change record in the CMDB, outside the validation package entirely —
shows version 14.4.2 as what actually got promoted to production during cutover. The guidance's
own instruction is to validate in a test environment and then move that exact configuration into
production (III.G). If the version tested isn't provably the version running now, the package's
"Pass" results don't tell you anything about the system Lakeshore actually operates. Nothing
inside the validation document would surface this — it only shows up when you cross-check it
against a second system of record, exactly the kind of check a non-technical reviewer has no
reason to make, and you do.
:::

## Where this goes next

You can now read executed evidence, not just a plan: tell a test that could fail from one that
never really tried, read a traceability matrix in both directions, and catch a version mismatch
a non-technical reviewer would miss entirely. What you haven't asked yet is a different question:
what *is* BECS, legally, and what does a vendor's clearance for Release B actually tell you about
the exact build running at Lakeshore? That's `becs-as-a-regulated-device`, next.
